title: Ignoring death after spawning misrepresents the population dynamics of marine semelparous species
content:
Life-history processes must be represented explicitly if population models are to provide credible support for resource management. By accounting for post-reproductive mortality, ACLS provides a biologically motivated framework for estimating population status and management-relevant quantities in semelparous species.


Abstract

Marine semelparous species are ecologically important and support major fisheries, with cephalopods and Pacific salmonids together contributing about 5% of global marine capture production. However, current stock assessment models were developed for iteroparous species and do not explicitly account for the post-reproductive mortality that defines semelparous life histories, which can bias estimation of population dynamics. We developed an age-structured statistical catch-at-length model for semelparity (ACLS) that explicitly removes mature individuals from subsequent timesteps after spawning. We tested ACLS in simulation experiments that covered contrasting semelparous life histories (squid and Pacific salmonids), alternative harvest pressures, environmental variability and stock–recruitment relationships. We also conducted sensitivity analyses to evaluate the performance of ACLS under misspecification of key life-history and fishery parameters. Further, we applied it to a case study for the jumbo squid Dosidicus gigas. ACLS consistently outperformed ACL in the simulation comparison between ACLS and ACL, improving the estimation of population dynamics and reducing bias across simulation scenarios. Sensitivity analyses showed that misspecification of key parameters, particularly natural mortality before post-reproductive mortality and maturity schedules, can affect the performance of ACLS. In the jumbo squid case study, all models fitted well and produced estimates of population dynamics that differed from those produced by the alternative assessment models. Ignoring post-reproductive mortality led to systematic overestimation of biomass in older age groups, particularly the post-reproductive cohort, which inflated spawning stock biomass estimates and distorted representation of population dynamics. In the jumbo squid case study, ACLS showed no evident retrospective bias, provided a satisfactory fit to catch, abundance-index and length-composition data, and differed markedly from SS3, ACL, SPiCT and CMSY in terms of key assessment outputs. Synthesis and applications. Life-history processes must be represented explicitly if population models are to provide credible support for resource management. By accounting for post-reproductive mortality, ACLS provides a biologically motivated framework for estimating population status and management-relevant quantities in semelparous species.
